title: The Man Who Counted Breaths (简体中文)
summary: An eccentric ascetic claims he can achieve immortality by counting every breath. Birbal reveals the absurdity of mechanical existence. [ZH]
full_text:
An eccentric yogi named Shvasananda arrived in Agra, boasting that he had discovered the secret of extended life. Standing before Emperor Akbar, he announced:

'Every human being is allotted exactly eight hundred million breaths by destiny! Most foolish mortals waste their breaths in laughing, shouting, running, and singing, exhausting their life in fifty years!

'I, however, count every inhale and exhale with mechanical precision, taking only four slow breaths every minute! In this manner, I shall live for three hundred years in perfect preservation!'

Akbar was intrigued: 'Is it true, Birbal? Can a man double his lifespan by counting his breaths?'

Birbal smiled: 'Let us test how much life he actually enjoys, Sire.'

Birbal invited the breath-counter to stay in the palace for three days.

During a magnificent musical performance by Mian Tansen that evening, when the entire court was swaying in ecstatic joy, Birbal watched the yogi. While everyone else smiled and wiped tears of bliss, the yogi sat rigid, eyes glazed, lips moving silently: 'One hundred... one hundred and one... one hundred and two...'

He could not listen to the music, for fear of losing his count!

At the royal banquet, when delicious saffron kebabs and sweet mangoes were served, the yogi chewed each bite with cold detachment, taking three minutes between breaths, refusing to laugh or converse.

On the third day, Birbal said to Emperor Akbar:

'Sire, observe this man. He breathes, his heart beats, and his lungs move like an iron blacksmith's bellows.

'Yet he does not enjoy music, he does not taste food, he does not love a friend, he does not smile at a child, and he does not wipe the tears of the suffering!

'He is not a living man; he is merely an animated corpse counting seconds in a tomb! What is the use of living three hundred years if those years are completely empty of joy, love, and virtue? Better to live fifty years of passionate service and deep love than three centuries of counting empty air.'

Akbar embraced Birbal's philosophy, declaring that life is measured by the depth of its moments, not by the number of its breaths.
